doc.title: Rick Margitza interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 22, 2024

title: Making 'Sacred Hearts' with his Paris quartet
summary: All original music recorded with his quartet in four days, overdubbed over four years, with no outside producer.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Okay how about — would you like to share something about I don’t know if this is your latest record, “Sacred Hearts.”

All original material, yeah. So the nucleus, the quartet on that record is the quartet that I work with here in Paris, and actually the drummer is one of my oldest friends from New Orleans named Jeff Boudreaux, who was in Paris before I was, also the bass player named Peter Giron is from New York in the Bronx. So three ex-pats and a French pianist, and we had been working together for the last five, six, seven years. So going in there and having my band and the music that we had been playing made it relatively stress-free. Because usually going into a recording studio can be kind of intimidating. But we just went in there and played our music and that’s the nucleus of the record. And I knew that after I had that stuff recorded my plan was to then overdub percussion and guitars and some keyboards and singing and so it’s kind of like we did the first round — I don’t want to say adding all the details made it go from color to black & white — I mean from black & white to color, because it wasn’t in black & white to begin with, but I feel like I went in there afterwards and then orchestrated it. And the tracks were done for a while and then the rest of the process took even longer so I think from the beginning to the end, the © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

whole record took almost four years, even though the majority of it was recorded in four days. The finishing of it and the mixing and mastering and orchestrating and bringing people in to do the overdubbing and all that was done in stages.
Did you have — well it could be a producer but I’m thinking of an outside ear to you know contribute that sound? Because sometimes it’s hard to be objective about your own work.

Absolutely it is. Not somebody who was in the studio working with me. I kind of had a general — because the record I made before that was kind of the same but the basic tracks were more world music influenced. This was more — I hate to compare it — it’s kind of like a Pat Metheny with saxophone sound, more kind of American, not as ethnic. So I had that first experience as an experience to help me, but then I would take certain tracks and then play it for the guys in the band or just snippets and say what does this sound like, what did you think? So that’s the only sounding board. I didn’t really have a producer other than me, and then when we finally got to the mix the engineer was really good so he had some insights into how things should just be panned and of course balanced and then he did have some suggestions for a couple of the arrangements, like maybe there are too many vocals at this point so we could thin them out here. So yeah. Mainly just kind of my own vision of what I wanted it to be.
